title: Engineering AI Discover
summary:
The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer

By Varun Khaitan, Peng Ren, Gary Tang, Itay Teller, Atif Faheem, Nipun Kumar, Donnie DeBoer, Eduardo Lundgren, Matteo Rinaldi, Raghav Bakshi

We recently introduced AI Discover, a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see.

Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline.

This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way.

Why an intelligence layer?

Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer.

The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design:

  1. Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused.
  2. Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent.
  3. Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not be what you asked for. So we use LLMs selectively, treat what they return as untrusted input and test performance and quality before anything ships.
  4. Adapting to fast-changing models, tools and prompts. Modeling and engineering solutions keep evolving, so the product can’t depend on any single model, tool or prompt.
  5. Building for TV. Typing on a TV is hard, so members rely on the remote, and the app should respond to every press right away on widely varying hardware. TV apps also update slowly, so changes have to ship without an app release. A typical TV request returns in moments, while multi-step generation can take several seconds.
  6. Holding a safety and reliability bar at scale. Members always get a page, even when an LLM call fails or yields poor results. Their choices and our content standards hold on every request, and when something breaks, structured records show why.
  7. Learning from what members say alongside what we already know. Recommendations have always learned from viewing behavior. AI Discover also lets members tell us what they want, and that has to shape what they see next.

System Architecture

When a member picks a theme, the TV app sends the request to the Page Server, which builds pages for all Netflix apps and hands the request asynchronously to the intelligence layer. At a high level, this new layer has two components: a controller and an executor.

The controller decides what to run. It gathers the context needed for each request, including real-time signals such as the time of day. It then settles on a plan, either an established one or a new one drafted by its planner, validates it and retrieves only the member details that this plan requires from Memory Hub, our per-member memory store. These details may include member taste summaries generated by MemberLLM, our in-house language model for personalized recommendations, or feedback shared by the member. We talk more about Memory Hub and member taste summaries later.

A plan is a graph of approved steps, each running a capability. A capability is a named unit of work that can have multiple versions and belongs to a family such as retrieval, ranking, generation or packaging. It declares its inputs and outputs, the context it may see and what happens if it fails.

Capability declarations make a plan verifiable. Before execution, the controller validates the graph: every step is approved, every input has a producer, nothing loops and the plan ends in exactly one page. Afterward, the controller checks the result before it’s served.

The executor runs the plan. Steps pass typed outputs to each other through the declared contracts, so each receives exactly what it asked for. Independent steps run in parallel, each with its own deadline and appropriate fallback behaviors. Some steps are optimized LLM calls with one task each, such as writing row titles or suggesting next themes, and they act only within the validated plan. Checks before the run and contracts during it give us governed execution, where every action stays within limits set in code.

Both parts write to the request records, the traces we use offline to evaluate and improve the system.

Key Decisions

Each challenge led to one decision. Here’s what we chose and what it bought us.

1. Design the product and architecture around LLMs

We reimagined the experience around LLMs. The easier path would have been to drop them in as rankers, keep today’s latency budgets and precompute where necessary. AI Discover is built on a back-and-forth around themes a member can steer, which gives LLMs work only they can do: generating themes, explaining rows, summarizing taste and helping choose the titles that fit the member and the moment. Members pick themes with the remote, so they never have to type. On the TV, those themes and explanations get their own native UI elements. Behind the screen, LLMs can draft plans, and asynchronous serving gives multi-step agentic orchestration the time it needs.

This opens up experiences our traditional stack couldn’t support on its own.

2. Make existing systems composable

Keeping recommendations grounded meant building on the systems that already know our catalog and members. Most capabilities wrap complex, proven Netflix systems such as search, large-scale ranking and catalog metadata access. Some of them may run their own agents in the future.

Reshaping them took careful work, because agentic orchestration challenges many long-standing assumptions of distributed systems. A capability now has to work in combinations no one designed, for a caller that chooses to call it at runtime. Each one needs a clear purpose and a semantic interface, and shaping it means deciding how much to combine into a single step and how much to leave to the planner. Too fine, and the planner has more ways to go wrong; too coarse, and it loses room to compose richer plans.

In return, the planner gets building blocks it can mix in new ways, and connecting services takes far less manual wiring. Because plans can only use these blocks, even one drafted on the fly stays grounded in our catalog and member taste.

3. Plan first, then execute

To contain LLM latency and errors, we plan every request before anything runs. The familiar way to let an agent use tools is a loop: reason, call a tool, read the result, reason again. It’s flexible, but you can’t tell up front how many steps it will take or whether it has gone down a wrong path. In agent terms, ours is a plan-and-execute agent: an LLM can propose the path, but code decides whether it runs.

Plans come from two places: established plans we’ve already tested, and plans an LLM drafts on the fly. A router we control decides which one is served. Either way, the plan passes the same checks before it runs. If the planner is slow or its plan fails a check, we fall back to a tested plan.

This allows for adaptive planning. The planner can find new ways to serve a request, and we can balance cost, latency and quality for each task, from a lean single-call plan to a richer multi-step one.

4. Stay model and capability agnostic

The best model or capability for a task today may be second-best, or overkill, in a few months, so we built the system to switch between them. We assign each task to the model or capability version that fits it. Today that’s a per-task setting we can override live. Only some steps in a request use an LLM.

That only works if switching is easy. All the LLMs we use sit behind one common interface. Before we switch, each candidate is scored on the same tasks by automated checks and LLM judges, so every swap is a measured change.

Much of the system’s behavior lives in server-side prompts and configuration, so we can swap models, tools and capabilities without new code or a TV app release.

Upgrades get cheap and experiments get easy. Moving to a better model, ranker or retrieval system is a plan or setting change, not a migration, so each component can keep improving without a large investment.

5. Make page generation asynchronous

Inference keeps getting faster, but member expectations rise just as quickly: richer responses, more context and more of the page shaped by LLMs. The line between what feels instant and what’s worth waiting for will keep shifting, so we built the asynchronous path as a first-class way of serving.

Most of a TV app is synchronous: press a button, get a page. Generative work breaks that pattern. Holding one request open for many seconds across services would tie up too many threads. So requests that involve generation are asynchronous. The press returns right away with an acknowledgement, and the TV switches to a thinking state that explains what’s being prepared. Meanwhile, the executor runs the plan in the background. When the result is ready, the server notifies the TV, which then fetches it.

Slow generation no longer slows anything else. The serving path stays healthy however long a turn takes, and every press still gets immediate feedback on screen.

6. Enforce safety in code

Some rules must hold no matter what an LLM writes: content and maturity standards, what each step can access, and what a member has asked us not to show them. Putting those rules in a prompt makes them probabilistic, so we enforce them in code. Generated text is cleaned up before it reaches the screen. The planner sees a stripped-down request, and member details are limited to what the validated plan needs.

For example, the planner decides which inputs each step needs, such as the profile’s maturity rating for retrieval. Instead of writing parameter values directly, it uses placeholders. After the plan passes validation, the controller fills them with values from the request, matched by declared type. This also protects against prompt injection.

Each request also leaves a structured record: the plan, each step and its outcome, and which rules applied. When a page misses, we can tell whether the plan, the data, a rule or the model was at fault. The same records feed our offline evaluation and replay.

Together, these rules and records let an experiment ship at the same safety and privacy bar as the rest of the product.

7. Remember what members tell us

A taste summary is a short profile of what a member enjoys, such as favorite genres, tone and recurring themes. MemberLLM generates it ahead of time from the member’s viewing history, which keeps that LLM work off the request path. It helps us further personalize their page, and steps that write themes and explanations receive it as context, so their wording reflects the member. We’ll cover MemberLLM in more detail in an upcoming post.

In AI Discover, members can also tune their recommendations and tell us directly what they want. Those choices apply right away and carry across visits, and they give us a new signal alongside what we already know about their taste. This is a first step toward remembering more about each member, from their preferences to the habits that show up over time and the corners of the catalog they like to explore. We keep it all in Memory Hub, our persistent, low-latency memory store, next to their taste summaries, and we can add new kinds of memory as we need them. We apply these memories to later requests where they’re relevant, together with real-time context.

The member holds the remote

In this version, members interact by selecting themes and using tuning options such as “don’t recommend.” There’s no free-text input or open-ended chat. That keeps the LLM’s job narrow by design.

  • The usual protections still apply. Profile settings and our safety and privacy policies hold here as everywhere else.
  • Generated text was tested before launch. We ran safety evaluations on theme labels, row titles and explanations to make sure they meet our standards.

What’s next

It would have been faster to let an LLM do everything and stop there. The intelligence layer gave us an AI-native product, grounded building blocks, adaptive planning, quicker experimentation, asynchronous generation, governed execution and agent memory for tunable personalization. While AI Discover is its first experience, we designed it with more in mind.

We’ve organized our efforts to answer two questions:

  • How much do members want to shape their recommendations? Whether they’d rather steer or lean back, and how much, which kinds of themes help, and how we should blend what members tell us with our existing personalization systems.
  • What tradeoffs does this technology bring? How cost and latency hold up in production as we ramp traffic, how long members will wait for generated results, and whether errors came from the model, the harness or our existing systems. Multi-turn sessions also need different evaluation and observability than single requests.

Longer term, our goal is a system that improves itself, starting from the record each request leaves behind. Today we replay past requests against a new prompt, model or rule to see what changes, and we judge each change with automated checks, LLM judges and human evaluations. Eventually, we want the system to propose improvements, test them safely and keep only what proves better, within our privacy and data-use policies. As LLMs improve, more of the work may move into them, and the intelligence layer lets us move that line deliberately.

This is part of a bigger shift. Recommendation systems have long learned quietly from what members watch and answered with ranked rows. LLMs let them listen and respond, and members may increasingly expect that. We’ll keep exploring what that means for discovery on Netflix.

title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems
summary: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.

title: Render the Robot, Generate the World: One Video World Model Across Embodiments
summary: Predicting the consequences of an agent's actions requires modeling both the body's motion and the environment's response. Most video world models attempt to learn both from numerical actions, even though geometry and kinematics already specify the intended motion. We introduce Doppel, an embodiment-agnostic video world model conditioned on camera-aligned renderings of future body configurations and numerical action trajectories. By explicitly providing the intended motion, Doppel can focus on predicting object motion and interaction-driven changes in the environment. Rendered motion also provides a common visual interface across different embodiments and action spaces. To train on robot datasets without camera extrinsics, we recover camera poses and align rendered trajectories with recorded observations. We jointly train a single shared video backbone and conditioning adapter on eight datasets spanning eight robot and human embodiments, from single- and bimanual robot arms to a dexterous humanoid and human hands and bodies, using about 600 hours of video without embodiment labels. Across three robot-arm datasets, Doppel improves PSNR over action-only baselines by 1.00 dB on held-out trajectories and 1.20 dB under out-of-distribution evaluation, while predicting more consistent object motion. title: Agentic Harness Engineering Beta: Requirement-Centered Evolution of Agent Harnesses
summary: Real-world harness engineering is driven by explicit and implicit user requirements, which guide development and validation. However, existing harness evolution methods often overlook implicit requirements and interaction needs, while using a single evolution agent to modify the harness and benchmark scores to select changes. This process often produces narrow patches and leads to benchmark-specific local optima. We introduce Agentic Harness Engineering Beta (AHE-Beta), a requirement-centered loop that brings real-world engineering practices into harness evolution. The loop consists of three steps: (1) User-driven evaluation lets simulated users raise their requirements as issues while they work with the harness over multiple turns. (2) Team-based modification implements those requirements as generalizable changes rather than task-specific patches. (3) Requirement-driven selection merges a change only when it resolves a verified requirement and passes review. Empirically, on held-out tasks, AHE-Beta raises pass@1 from 21.9% to 33.3% while using 40.8% fewer tokens than Base Harness, and achieves higher pass@1 than Claude Code, Meta-Harness, and AHE. In a blind human A/B test, real users prefer AHE-Beta in 31 of 48 valid pairs and rate it higher on all five dimensions, matching the directional preference of the user simulator. The human A/B results show that AHE-Beta achieves its goal of aligning harness evolution with real-world user requirements. Without further evolution, the gains transfer to GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with pass@1 improvements of 15.8% and 5.3% over Base Harness. Together, these results show that requirement-centered harness evolution is a more general method for improving agent capabilities.

title: PrismRestore: A Compact Restoration Toolbox for Agentic Image Restoration
summary: Agentic image restoration composes operations to handle mixed degradations, yet its toolbox often requires storing multiple restoration networks. An offline task-prior search uses activation and gradient statistics to group channels with similar response profiles, then searches task-specific modulation coefficients over non-representative channels while leaving representative channels unmodulated. Experiments on synthetic composite-degradation and real-world multi-task benchmarks show improvements over the evaluated all-in-one baselines and restoration quality competitive with multi-model agents. title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents
summary: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities.

title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity
summary: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait.

title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. title: Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves.

title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. title: Communications-free Collective Intelligence Via Allocentric Belief
summary: A team of skilled card players share no information amongst each other, and yet still are able to coordinate their play by watching the same players and reading the same tells. Autonomous systems have failed to exploit this logic, relying instead on explicit communication or complex state estimation schemes that can fail when it matters most. Without it, decentralized agents diverge in their world beliefs, and coordination collapses. Here we show that anchoring all agents to a single shared external actor, a common witness whose reactions encode team state, produces spontaneous, communication-free coordination. An allocentric belief network trained on witness behavior allows each agent to independently reconstruct full team state, keeping group beliefs consistent with no inter-agent exchange. Across five competitive environments allocentric belief alignment outperforms egocentric approaches in collective performance, and even scales to sixty-agent teams where standard methods fail. These results establish a new principle for collective intelligence: in the absence of communication, a shared gaze replaces a shared channel.

summary: Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. summary: Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. title: Kaer: Security-Aware Replanning for Multi-Agent Systems
summary:

Although entire exemplars function as an intuitive baseline for prototype-based explanations, we highlight prototypical parts as particularly valuable for tabular data. By grouping related features into bounded subspaces, prototypical parts technically embody human-understandable concepts, replacing isolated features with cohesive semantic units. Cognitively, these parts align with Rosch's categorization theory and Kahneman's System 1 thinking to naturally reduce cognitive load for humans. Then, we introduce a Geometric Validity Triad to conceptualize why prototypes validate the data manifold - a critical dimension often neglected by existing methods. We contend that making tabular XAI genuinely comprehensible requires shifting toward composite explanation pipelines that pair intuitive similarity-based reasoning with rigorous feature-level auditing. The paper concludes by outlining open challenges of prototype-based methods and discussing potential solutions to guide future research.

title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. title: A Homogeneous Benchmark of Exoplanet Mass-Radius Relations
summary: The mass-radius ($M$-$R$) relation is fundamental to inferring the bulk composition and internal structure of exoplanets. However, published relations remain difficult to compare directly because studies adopt different planetary samples, fitting procedures, and evaluation metrics. On the full test set, a multi-feature random forest has the lowest root-mean-square error, 0.329~dex in $\log_{10} M$ versus 0.368~dex for a fitted two-parameter power law ($p = 0.007$ unadjusted; $p = 0.059$ after Holm correction across 13 comparisons). Radius-only ML models perform comparably to the single power law. In three ranges of the measured radius, several methods improve on the power law below 1.6 $R_\oplus$, but none does between 1.6 and 4 $R_\oplus$. Including stellar and orbital covariates significantly improves predictions only for low-mass planets ($M < 4.4\,M_\oplus$), although this result is sensitive to missing covariate data and weakens when the training and test sets are separated by host star. Within their calibrated radius domains, the published empirical and probabilistic relations remain highly competitive. Finally, a first-order variance decomposition shows that formal measurement uncertainties account for only $\sim$3\% of the residual variance (0.067 of 0.401~dex), and the remaining $\sim$0.396~dex arises from compositional diversity, selection effects, and model approximation error.

title: xTBloom: GPU Batching for High-Throughput GFN-xTB Calculations
summary: Conformational searches and multiwindow free-energy sampling require large numbers of GFN-xTB energy and force evaluations across molecular conformations and sampling windows. These results demonstrate the throughput benefits of batched GFN-xTB evaluation for repeated electronic-structure calculations and multiwindow sampling.

title: MLIR-MRacle: Memory-Model-Aware Metamorphic Fuzzing of Concurrent MLIR
summary: Multi-level compilers built on MLIR lower concurrent programs through many stages towards targets with potentially drastically different memory models, where an optimisation which appears reasonable, can silently change program behaviour. Testing these lowerings is hard: a concurrent program often has no single expected outcome, and existing MLIR fuzzers often assume determinism. We present MLIR-MRacle, a memory-model-aware metamorphic fuzzer for concurrent MLIR programs. MLIR-MRacle applies metamorphic relations gated by the target memory model, so that both the original and transformed programs remain well defined - executing both repeatedly, and comparing their outcome sets or distributions withone of two statistical oracles. A coverage guided campaign driver built on libafl is used to perform continuous fuzzing. MRs, memory models, oracles, and execution backends all provide extension points for future researchers and compiler engineers to build off this package. In a case study on Armv8 hardware, MLIR-MRacle ran over 145k trials across four configurations, reaching up to 93.6k compiler coverage edges, and found a bug in the OpenMP dialect verifier that has since been fixed upstream. title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
summary: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.

title: Asteroseismology of AI Velorum: a prototype of high-amplitude delta Scuti stars
summary:
AI Velorum is exceptional among high-amplitude δScuti (HADS) stars because of its multimode pulsations. Despite being an excellent target for asteroseismology, this prototype star has not been studied in detail.
  We determine the stellar parameters, age, and evolutionary stage of AI Vel, constrain envelope convection and convective core overshooting, and test three opacity data sets: OPAL, OP, and OPLIB.
  We analysed TESS photometry, ground-based Strömgren photometry, and HARPS spectroscopy. Modes were identified using photometric and spectroscopic methods, and empirical values of the non-adiabatic f-parameter were derived for both radial modes. Seismic modelling was performed within a Bayesian framework supported by Monte Carlo simulations.
  We confirm the radial nature of the two dominant modes and identify one non-radial mode as most likely an axisymmetric dipole or quadrupole mode. Within the explored parameter space, only OPAL models reproduce the observed position of AI Vel in the HR diagram, whereas OP and OPLIB models are too cool and underluminous. All seismic models favour inefficient envelope convection (mixing-length parameter alpha_{mlt}\lesssim 0.5). Including the non-radial mode substantially reduces the formal posterior uncertainties, but the ambiguity in its identification introduces additional model-dependent uncertainties. AI Vel is an evolved, slowly rotating star in the hydrogen shell-burning phase.
  Our results demonstrate the diagnostic power of combining pulsation frequencies with empirical f-parameters. The preference for OPAL opacities is consistent with results for several other HADS and SX Phoenicis stars but does not imply a general superiority of OPAL opacities.

title: Ultimate3D: Teaching Multimodal LLMs 3D Camera-Object Relations by Large-Scale Visual Instruction Data
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with accurately capturing camera-object relations, especially for object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera shots. title: Exploring Speaker-Aware Engagement Modeling for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
summary: Prior work on engagement modeling in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has demonstrated substantial individual variability in behavioral features, particularly in visual modalities. In this work, we extend the literature to acoustic features in naturalistic interactions, where multiple speakers and atypical interaction patterns complicate speaker-specific analysis. We trained classical machine learning models using acoustic features extracted from diarized child and parent/caregiver audio and compared their performance with models trained on undiarized audio. Diarized audio consistently yielded higher area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values, although these differences were not statistically significant. More importantly, the relative contributions of child and caregiver acoustic features varied across participants, indicating that the acoustic information associated with engagement was not consistent across children. These findings extend evidence of participant-level variability in ASD engagement modeling to the acoustic domain and demonstrate the feasibility of isolating speaker-specific vocalizations for studying engagement in complex, naturalistic interactions.

title: The Elephant in the Question: Unified Models Picture the Concepts Behind Their Answers
summary: Visualizing intermediate representations could help us inspect the reasoning steps underlying a model output. Unified multimodal models offer this opportunity by combining understanding and generation in one architecture. Their image generators can access representations formed while processing text. We introduce the V-lens, which uses this connection to visualize a chosen token's hidden state without training a decoder. Across four diffusion-based and two purely autoregressive unified models, the resulting images reveal key intermediate concepts that connect a question to its answer even when the concepts are never named explicitly. Controlled tests show how this content changes with context, token position, and depth. We then introduce lens tuning, which supervises selected hidden states with pictures through the V-lens. Across BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and HunyuanImage-3.0, the rate of correct visualizations of pronoun referents rises from 2-11% to 86-94%. Surprisingly, such visual supervision also improves text answers without supervising the answer tokens directly. Code is available at https://github.com/multimodal-ai-lab/V-lens.

title: Towards Transparent Computational Agents for Air Traffic Control: Explainability, Interpretability and Trust
summary: We report preliminary findings from an ongoing investigation into transparency techniques for computational Air Traffic Control agents. title: LLM-Guided Cyber-Physical Attack Path Identification in Smart Grids
summary: Identifying high-impact attack paths in cyber-physical power systems is critical for improving grid resilience. Existing methods typically rely on either structural topology analysis or simulation-based cascading-failure models. Topology-based approaches capture connectivity but lack adversarial reasoning, while simulation-driven methods are primarily suited for offline analysis and are less effective for rapid evaluation of evolving attack scenarios. As a result, identifying realistic attack paths that jointly capture topology, threat semantics, and physical impact remains challenging. This paper presents a physics-grounded framework for identifying cyber-physical attack paths using large language models (LLMs), with cascading-failure-derived impact rankings used as physics-grounded references. The framework integrates system topology, LLM-guided STRIDE and MITRE ATT&CK threat modeling, and three baseline strategies for comparison: topology-driven, threat-driven, and fusion-based. Evaluation is performed using (i) critical-node overlap between LLM-inferred top-K rankings and cascading-failure-based ground truth; (ii) node-level similarity between LLM-inferred and reference paths; and (iii) path-level alignment capturing agreement in complete attack sequences. Results show that structured LLM-based threat modeling substantially improves alignment with physics-grounded references. In the cyber layer, critical-node overlap@3 increases from approximately 33% to as high as 100%, while node-level similarity reaches up to 65% and path-level alignment reaches up to 48%. In addition, the proposed framework reduces runtime by approximately 75--85% compared to the fusion-based baseline in the IEEE 14-bus system. These results suggest that LLM-guided attack path identification is a promising approach for efficient and impact-aware cyber-physical security analysis.
